title: Laser-Induced 90-Degree Magnetization Switching for Single-Element 2D Sensing
authors: Floris J. F. van Riel, Niels F. L. van Kempen, Bert Koopmans, Diana C. Leitao
abstract: Magnetoresistive sensors with multiaxial sensitivity are interesting for field mapping applications where local measurement of multiple magnetic field components is needed. Existing device designs are often discretized with separate sensing elements for each vector component, or they require complex detection schemes to distinguish the different components. In this work, we showcase a single-element two-dimensional vector sensor with on-demand reprogrammable sensing axis using light and optically switchable materials. Our device is an anisotropic magnetoresistive sensor with $90^\circ$ togglable sensitivity upon excitation with ultrashort laser pulses. The sensor consists of an optically switchable Co/Gd thin-film bilayer, patterned into a cross shape that stabilizes two orthogonal in-plane magnetization directions. By selectively addressing one diagonal of the cross, a single laser pulses toggle switches the magnetization direction in the center of the cross by $90^\circ$. Moreover, the field sensitivity of the device is toggled between the $x$- and $y$-axes, which we detected electrically with the planar Hall effect. Our results form a milestone towards optically reprogrammable integrated magnetic vector sensors.
summary: This work presents a novel, single-element magnetic vector sensor that uses an optically switchable thin-film bilayer patterned into a cross shape. By applying a short laser pulse, the device's magnetization can be switched by 90 degrees, enabling the electrical measurement of magnetic field components along two orthogonal axes. This demonstrates a significant step toward integrated, reprogrammable magnetic sensing technology.
main_problem: The goal is to create a single-element, two-dimensional magnetic vector sensor capable of reprogrammably switching its sensing axis on demand using light.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a proof-of-principle device where a single laser pulse can toggle the magnetization direction by 90 degrees, allowing the electrical measurement of field sensitivity along orthogonal axes (x and y).
method: The study combines electrical characterization (AMR and PHE measurements) with theoretical modeling (macrospin and micromagnetic simulations) to predict and verify the switching behavior.
model_or_system: The physical system is an anisotropic magnetoresistive (AMR) sensor built from an optically switchable Co/Gd thin-film bilayer patterned into a cross shape. The behavior is modeled using macrospin approximations and micromagnetic simulations.
key_observables: AMR signal ($\Deltaho/ho_\perp$), Planar Hall Effect (PHE) signal ($ho_{xy}$), and the angle-dependent field sensitivity along the x and y axes.
important_parameters: Laser pulse energy ($\sim 2 \mu	ext{J}$), laser fluence threshold ($\gtrsim 10 	ext{ mJ cm}^{-2}$), and the magnetic anisotropy constants.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on macrospin approximations for field response and assumes that the measured resistance changes are dominated by the patterned magnetic film.
figures_summary: Figures show the crossed ellipse geometry, AMR response curves for sweeping fields along x and y axes, and time evolution of magnetization during optical switching.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from introducing the need for vector sensors to detailing the device structure, presenting electrical measurements of AMR/PHE, and finally supporting these findings with detailed macrospin and micromagnetic simulations of the 90-degree switching mechanism.
why_interesting: While primarily in condensed matter spintronics, the use of ultrafast laser pulses to deterministically switch magnetic states is highly relevant to the field of quantum optics and open quantum systems, particularly in controlling magnetic moments.

Solid lines are sinusoidal fits of the measured points. A current of 1 mA was used.

FIG. 4. Demonstration of 90◦optical switching of the central part of the CE using PHE and a current of 100 µA a.c. With the device initially in the M →state (a), there is no response to an Hx field. After illumination with a single laser pulse, the device is in the M ↑state (b) and there is a positive linear response to Hx. On the other hand, starting in the M ←state (c) with no Hx response, after laser excitation the device ends up in the M ↓state (d) with negative linear Hx response. The dotted lines are the expected slopes based on measurements of the M ↑and M ↓states after manual setting with a permanent magnet.
